event: Elsie wakes in the attic room to bread-smell and lake mist on the round window.
She has been awake a while, listening to the ovens below and turning the day over.
She sits up, and greets the four plants on the sill first, each one by name.
She washes at the cold basin and stands a moment in the little room in her shift.
She laces the cream halter top of her novice's outfit with fingers that are not steady.
The pink-and-white flower clip goes above one ear; she checks it twice in the tin mirror.
She writes the week's letter to her mother at the little table, and seals it.
She counts her coins onto the blanket, then puts them back in the belt pouch.
She checks the healer's satchel: bandages, honey salve, the brown tincture.
Elsie eats a warm roll in the bakery standing up, and the baker waves her out.
The canal is under mist, and the arched bridges come out of it one by one.
Elsie posts the letter at the corner shop and watches it drop through the slot.
Two women go by arm in arm, and the street takes no notice of them at all.
The Hall of Naming stands white above the lake, its glass dome full of morning.
Twenty-year-olds gather on the steps in knots, dressed as well as their houses can.
The girl ahead of Elsie in the line asks if she is nervous, and Elsie says yes.
The girl says her hands are cold, and Elsie takes one and holds it warm a moment.
Inside, the dome lifts every whisper, and the silver circle waits in the floor.
A priestess in white begins to call the names from a long list.
The first girl steps alone into the circle, and the hall holds its breath.
The System's window opens above her, and the whole hall reads her class and claps.
Elsie watches the windows come and go, and hopes for simples and bandages.
When it is her turn she goes up the three steps into the circle, and stands still.
The window opens above her, large enough for a whole hall to read.
It reads: Enthraller.
Elsie reads it twice, the way you read a word in a language you are still learning.
The silence spreads outward from the circle, and nobody in the hall moves.
In the gallery a woman rises and takes her child by the hand and goes out.
The priestess has gone the colour of the walls and has not called the next name.
Elsie says: Oh! That sounds like a lot of responsibility.
She smiles at the frightened priestess, and steps down out of the circle.
The hall does not clap.
On the steps outside, the others from the line have become strangers, looking at her and away.
She walks down from the hall alone, and the city is warm and ordinary around her.
The guild hall is timber and noise, its green copper roof across Brightwater Square.
Elsie waits in the registration line with the others who were Named this morning.
The clerk takes her name, and asks her class without looking up from the page.
Elsie says Enthraller, and the clerk's pen stops on the page.
The clerk looks up at last, then at the charcoal door, and stands and goes upstairs.
Elsie waits; the line behind her has quietly become a different line.
The guildmaster comes down: grey-haired, in her fifties, sleeves rolled, hands sword-calloused.
She looks at Elsie for a long moment, then asks her up to the office.
She reads the Strings Accord aloud and slowly, so that there is no misunderstanding.
Registered; every skill written down and reported; no skill on anyone who has not agreed.
Elsie asks whether the watching is so that nothing goes wrong, and is told it is.
She says then she is glad of it, and the guildmaster puts the paper away and rubs her eyes.
Elsie counts the registration fee onto the desk in silver and copper.
The clerk stamps a small copper tag with her name and an F, and hands it across.
The guildmaster says there is one more thing, and opens the charcoal-painted door.
A young woman is standing in the Warden's room with a black ledger shut in her hands.
Warden Corisande Vane, called Cora, is tall, in a charcoal coat buttoned to the throat.
The guildmaster says Cora will go with her on guild business, and write down every skill.
Cora says she will report each one to the guildmaster, and looks at Elsie while she says it.
Elsie says thank you for coming, and that it must be a great deal of walking.
Cora does not answer that.
Elsie asks what she likes in her tea.
Cora looks at her, and then says: black and strong, one sugar.
She answers at once, and Elsie has the feeling the question is a new one.
Elsie says she will remember that, and means it.
Back in the hall, the quest board runs its length, notices sorted from F up to S.
Elsie reads the F-rank notices twice, then finds the party board at the far end.
Parties chalk their names on slates and look each other over, and nobody looks at her.
She asks three slates in a row for a place, and each of them is full.
The fourth does not answer at all, and a woman turns the slate to the wall.
Down at the bottom corner of the board, four slates stand where the cast-offs post.
A woman is arguing with one of them, a great axe strapped across her back.
She tells Elsie the slate is hers, and that she may have the half she has not used.
Elsie asks about the axe; the woman says that is Margery, and they were thrown out together.
Tamsin tells it in a rush: the Copper Hounds dropped her this morning, before breakfast.
She says the shield-bearer's arm, and looks away, and laughs, and the laugh is wrong.
Elsie puts her hand flat on Tamsin's wrist, the way she does, and means it kindly.
Tamsin goes still under it, and then makes a joke of it, and her ears are red.
Elsie asks whether the arm is mending; Tamsin stares at her, and says probably.
A small woman in brass goggles has come out from behind a crate of notices.
Ottilie Brandt, called Tilly, talks fast and apologises before anything has gone wrong.
She was thrown out of the Alchemists' College last week, over the east lab windows.
Elsie asks what she brews; the answer takes four minutes and includes three warnings.
Tilly goes red to the ears when Elsie smiles at her, and drops her chalk twice.
Tamsin pulls a folded guild notice from her jerkin: moonbells, at the Glasswood's edge.
Six lanterns for the apothecary, and it is the one job nobody else wanted.
Elsie says the three of them could take it; Tamsin asks if she has been in a dungeon.
Elsie says she has not; Tamsin says good, neither has Tilly, and starts to laugh.
Tilly finds a chalk and holds it out, because the idea was Elsie's and the chalk is hers.
Elsie chalks three names on the last slate at the bottom corner of the board.
Tilly writes hers under Elsie's in smaller letters, and dots the i twice.
Tamsin adds hers last, in big ragged capitals, and stands back to look at it.
The guildmaster watches from the balcony above with her arms folded.
Elsie looks up and waves; the guildmaster waves back slowly, and goes in.
Tilly asks what class she is, and the talk around the slate goes quiet.
Elsie says Enthraller, and watches their faces, and does not look away.
Tamsin lifts her head, then says, so you can make me do anything, and laughs first.
Elsie says that is not how hers works, and that she does not know yet how it works.
Tilly asks a hundred questions about bonds and answers several of them herself.
Cora watches the wrist, the chalk, the red ears, and writes none of it down.
The lamplighters' boats move along the canal, and the lanterns come on one by one.
Elsie thinks the three of them are going to be friends, and is glad enough to hum.
Cora opens the black ledger at last, and looks at the blank first page.
She writes nothing in it, and closes it, and puts it back under her coat.
Elsie asks what she will write; Cora says she has not decided.
Elsie says she will try to give her something good to write.
